idiom_name: metadata store + metadata reader + generic mapping engine
implementation_notes: Language-neutral skeleton: declare the correspondence between class fields and table columns once, in a machine-readable store (a tabular declaration, mapping file, attribute set or schema definition), then read that store at startup or generation time into descriptors (field name, column name, type, key/generated flag, relationship) and let one engine perform read, insert and update by iterating the descriptors. The engine must be class-agnostic: it resolves the descriptor set for a class, builds the SQL and binds or materialises values; anything class-specific belongs in the metadata, or the engine degenerates into a hand-written mapper with extra steps. Where the language offers no reflection the same structure is built from static descriptor tables (column name, struct offset, size) and macros; where it offers code generation the reader is a generator and the descriptors are compiled code.
code_sketch:
metadata = load(mapping)                          # columns, types, keys, relations
for cls in metadata.classes:
    registry[cls] = descriptors(metadata, cls)     # once, at startup
def load(cls, row):                                # generic: no per-class code
    obj = cls()
    for d in registry[cls]:
        setattr(obj, d.field, convert(d.type, row[d.column]))
    return obj
pitfalls: Skipping the reader and letting each class interpret its own metadata rebuilds exactly the duplication the pattern removes.
Re-reading the metadata for every row turns a declarative mapping into a runtime hot path.
Metadata that is never generated from, or validated against, the schema will drift silently.

Wrong move: leave a hand-written mapper authoritative while treating metadata as decoration -> two sources of truth drift -> instead make the generic engine consume the descriptor set and validate it against the schema.
Wrong move: inspect annotations for every row -> reflection overhead turns mapping metadata into a hot path -> instead materialise and cache descriptors once per class.

Wrong move: trust convention-derived names after renaming a class or field -> reads and writes target the wrong table or column -> instead pin explicit names and fail startup when metadata disagrees with the schema.
